I just got a volume license, in a pack of 10. This comes with 50 activations. How do these activations work? If I activate a computer then re-image it and activate it again will this use one or two MAK activations?

from what I understand is that if you get audited you'll have to provide a count for the number of active computers running that license key, what I usually do when I'm imaging PCs is that I don't put the license key until I'm done with the image and even then I run sysprep(up to win7) and enter the key only when I know I have a workable image.

even then, if you pass the 50 activations all you need to do is call MS and they'll ask you for some numbers and "unlock" or reset the number of activations.

BUT I might be wrong so better to call MS and get the correct answer
This has been my experience as well. Activations are not tracked, but the audit is where they make sure numbers match.
How long are the licenses good for? I noticed that the expiry date on my account is 2 years from now.

MAK is a Multiple Activation Key. The number of activations are kept up with to some extent because in the Microsoft Volume Licensing Service Center products I have a MAK for will display as used/available (10/50 - If I had 50 licenses and had activated an OS or product on 10 machines).

If you re-image a computer and activate the license on the same machine again it wont count against the total because of the computers unique identifier.

If you're talking about your license agreement in the Microsoft Volume Licensing Service Center displaying as expiring in two years, pretty sure that's referring to the Software Assurance period.

A lot of factors come in to play when dealing with Microsoft Volume Licensing. There are several types of license agreement plans and types. Each can vary from relationship agreement to relationship agreement.

xlogicx is right on here. I've never seen a license for Windows 'expire' - the Software Assurance expires with your licensing agreement, but you purchased those licenses. They don't expire.

I told my brother-in-law that I think this is the catalyst for other services to follow. It didn't seem like it took long for CBS to come out with their "All Access" service, then Dish Network came out months back with a new service they'll be offering called "Sling TV". It feels like the behemoth content providers are finally showing signs that they understand the old paradigm of over 9000 channels for $300/month isn't in demand anymore. People want to watch a select group of shows or channels, at their convenience not a predetermined schedule, cheaply, and on whatever device they choose.

I am one of those cord-cutters. I haven't had any cable or satellite for nearly 5 years, I just watch local stations and Netflix. It always baffles the door-to-door sales kids that come around and try to get me to sign up. "You don't pay for cable/dish? Well...do you even watch TV?"

At this point, the only thing lagging is live sports. WatchESPN is a good first step, but still requires a cable subscription. Once live events, like sporting events, are broadcast without a cable subscription, then cable may finally not be a necessity for so many people anymore.
